name: Stillman diet

lead: The Stillman diet is a short-term plan created by physician Irwin Maxwell Stillman and described in the 1967 book The Doctor's Quick Weight Loss Diet, co-written with Samm Sinclair Baker. It allows lean animal protein, eggs and non-fat cottage cheese and excludes fruit, vegetables, bread, sugar, alcohol and added fats, with at least eight glasses of water daily.

People use it to lose body fat quickly, which makes the face leaner and the body look more defined. Published research is small: a 1974 JAMA study examined changes in serum cholesterol during the diet, and medical commentators have called it a fad diet.

paras: Followers eat six small meals of permitted foods a day, prepared without added fat, and drink plenty of water. Spices, tea, coffee and non-caloric drinks are allowed.

Critics note the diet is very low in fiber, vitamins and minerals, and a 1983 physician review described fatigue, nausea and possible deficiency with long use and reported higher serum cholesterol. People with medical conditions are generally advised to consult a clinician before restrictive diets.

angle.text: The diet is used for fast weight loss. People pursuing a leaner face and sharper physique use it as a short crash approach, usually for a limited time.

lead: The Stillman diet is a high-protein, low-carbohydrate plan devised by physician Irwin Maxwell Stillman (1896-1975) and popularised by the 1967 book The Doctor's Quick Weight Loss Diet, co-authored with Samm Sinclair Baker [1]. It is an early example of the low-carbohydrate fad-diet wave that preceded the Atkins diet; unlike Atkins, it limits fat as well [1].

The appearance goal is rapid fat loss: a leaner face, a visible jawline and a slimmer midsection. Followers eat six small meals daily of lean beef, veal, chicken, turkey, fish, eggs and non-fat cottage cheese, drink at least eight glasses of water, and avoid bread, fruit, sugar, alcohol and added fats [1].
Research is limited. A 1974 JAMA report examined serum cholesterol during the diet [2], and nutrition commentators have criticised it as a fad diet that is low in fiber and micronutrients [1].

paras: Permitted foods are lean beef, veal, chicken, turkey, fish, eggs and non-fat cottage cheese, with spices, herbs, salt, pepper and Tabasco sauce. Fats, oils, butter, dressings, bread, fruit, sugar and alcohol are excluded. Tea, coffee and non-caloric soft drinks are allowed in addition to water [1].

Stillman developed the plan in the 1960s from his New York practice and published it in 1967; it gained popularity in the late 1960s [1]. His 1975 New York Times obituary described him as the author of four popular diet books [1]. Singer Karen Carpenter began the diet as a teenager in 1967; Wikipedia reports this fact without attributing her later death from anorexia complications to the diet [1].

A 1974 JAMA study, Changes in serum cholesterol during the Stillman diet, followed participants on the regimen [2]. A summary of that work reports an average rise in serum cholesterol in a small group of participants over about a week [3]. A 1983 physician review stated that studies showed the diet raises serum cholesterol and that long-term use may cause vitamin deficiency [1].
Physician Terrence Kuske (1983) wrote that the diet induces diuresis and may cause fatigue, nausea and exhaustion [1]. Medical experts and nutritionists have classed it among fad diets [1].
